sections.title: The song that made people younger
sections.intro_md:
In 2011 three young psychologists published an experiment showing that listening to a Beatles song made people a year and a half younger. Not feel younger. Be younger, by their recorded date of birth. The statistics were clean. The result passed the test every psychology journal used.

It was a deliberate trap. Joseph Simmons, Leif Nelson and Uri Simonsohn had run the study honestly and analysed it the way many of their colleagues did: try a few measures, add a control variable here, stop collecting data when the numbers look good, report only what worked. Their point was that ordinary, accepted habits could prove something impossible.

That same year a respected journal published nine experiments claiming that students could sense the future, and a Dutch star of social psychology confessed to inventing data for years. Psychology had to ask an uncomfortable question: how many of its famous findings were true? Today is about how a claim gets tested, how that machinery broke, and how it is being rebuilt.

spotlights.name: When I'm Sixty-Four makes you younger
spotlights.spot_it: A deliberately absurd experiment that used ordinary statistics to prove the impossible.
spotlights.story_md: Twenty University of Pennsylvania students heard either the Beatles' 'When I'm Sixty-Four' or a control instrumental. Then they gave their birth dates. After adjusting for their fathers' age, the Beatles listeners came out about 1.5 years younger, with p = .04, under the conventional .05 bar. The authors then showed how they got there: they had measured many things, tried several analyses and peeked at the data as it came in. Their simulations found that combining four such common choices could push the chance of a false positive from the promised 5% to about 61%. They ended with six simple rules for authors, starting with: decide when you will stop collecting data before you begin.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It proved that the problem was not a few cheats but everyday habits.
spotlights.memory_hook: Paul McCartney cannot make you younger, but flexible statistics can.

spotlights.name: Feeling the Future
spotlights.spot_it: Nine experiments in a flagship journal that claimed students could sense pictures before they appeared.
spotlights.story_md: Daryl Bem, a Cornell social psychologist, ran classic experiments in reverse. In one, students guessed which of two curtains on a screen hid a picture. When the picture was erotic, they picked the right curtain 53.1% of the time, where chance is 50%. Eight of his nine experiments came out 'significant'. The Journal of Personality and Social Psychology published them in 2011 because the methods were standard. That was the scandal: if standard methods could prove precognition, the methods were the problem. The journal then declined to publish a failed replication, saying it did not run replications. A different journal, PLOS ONE, published three failed attempts in 2012.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It showed that passing the usual tests did not mean a finding was real.
spotlights.memory_hook: If the rules let ESP in, the rules are broken.

spotlights.name: Kahneman's 'train wreck' email
spotlights.spot_it: An open letter from a Nobel laureate warning his own field of a coming collision.
spotlights.story_md: Daniel Kahneman, the psychologist who won the 2002 Nobel prize in economics, had built a bestseller, 'Thinking, Fast and Slow', partly on priming studies: experiments where a subtle cue, like words about old age, supposedly changed behaviour. In September 2012 he emailed priming researchers: 'I see a train wreck looming.' He urged them to set up a 'daisy chain' of labs, each replicating another's results. Few did. In 2017 Kahneman wrote that he had placed too much faith in underpowered studies, and that readers should not trust the priming chapter of his own book the way he once asked them to.
spotlights.why_it_matters: A founder of the field said out loud that its evidence needed checking.
spotlights.memory_hook: The man who taught the world about bias admitted his own.

sections.title: What replication means, and the numbers that matter
sections.intro_md:
A **replication** is doing an experiment again, with new people, to see if the result comes back. It is the scientific version of 'show me again'. A **direct** replication copies the method as closely as possible. A **conceptual** replication tests the same idea a different way. Scientists also separate **reproducibility** (same data, same analysis, same answer) from **replicability** (new data, same answer).

For most of the 20th century, psychology journals rarely published direct replications. They wanted novelty. So nobody knew how often famous effects would survive a second look. Then, from 2011, large teams started counting. The answer, repeated across projects with different methods, was sobering: roughly half of published findings in social and behavioural science hold up when repeated, and the ones that do usually come back weaker.

The numbers below are the ones to remember. Note that 'failed to replicate' does not mean 'proved false'. It means the second, usually larger, test did not find the effect.

spotlights.spot_it: 270 researchers, 100 studies, one Science paper that became the field's reference number.
spotlights.story_md: Brian Nosek, a University of Virginia psychologist, organised volunteers to repeat 100 experiments published in 2008 in three leading journals. Teams contacted the original authors for materials and preregistered their plans. Of the original studies, 97 had reported significant results. Only 35 of 97 replications, 36%, were significant. Average effect sizes fell by about half. Cognitive psychology did better (about half replicated) than social psychology (about a quarter). The paper, published in Science on 28 August 2015, did not say the failures were false. It said, in its own words, that there was still more work to do to verify whether we know what we think we know.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It replaced anecdotes about bad studies with a measured rate.
spotlights.memory_hook: One hundred studies in, a third came out again.

spotlights.name: Many Labs: the same experiment in 36 countries
spotlights.spot_it: Dozens of labs run identical short experiments at once, so a result cannot hide behind one sample.
spotlights.story_md: Many Labs 1 (2014) ran 13 classic effects in 36 samples and 6,344 people. Ten replicated clearly, including anchoring and framing. Two priming effects, flag priming and money priming, did not. Many Labs 2 (2018) went bigger: 28 findings, 125 samples, 15,305 people in 36 countries and territories. Fifteen came back significant in the original direction. The median effect shrank from d = 0.60 to 0.15. A key surprise: when an effect was real, it mostly appeared everywhere, and when it failed, it failed everywhere. So 'it only works in some cultures' rarely rescued a failed result.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It killed the excuse that replications fail because the new sample is different.
spotlights.memory_hook: Same test, 36 countries: real effects travel, phantom ones vanish everywhere.

sections.title: How psychology tests a claim
sections.intro_md:
Suppose someone claims that holding a warm cup of coffee makes you judge strangers as warmer people. How would you test it?

First, turn the idea into something measurable: hand people a hot or iced cup, then have them rate a stranger on a scale. Second, **randomly assign** people to the hot or cold group, so that the groups differ only by chance. Third, keep the person running the study **blind** to which group is which, so they cannot nudge anyone. Fourth, decide in advance how many people to test, which needs a guess at how big the effect is. Then run the study and ask: is the difference between groups bigger than chance alone would usually produce?

That last question is where the **p-value** comes in, and where most of the trouble starts. The tools below are each simple. The crisis came from how they were combined, bent and misread. (The warm-cup finding, published in Science in 2008, failed in larger replications in 2014.)

spotlights.name: Peirce and Jastrow randomise by playing cards
spotlights.spot_it: Two Americans testing whether people can sense tiny weight differences, with a shuffled pack deciding the order.
spotlights.story_md: Charles Sanders Peirce and his student Joseph Jastrow wanted to know if people could detect weight differences too small to consciously notice. Jastrow sat behind a screen judging weights while Peirce set them. To stop either of them from creating a pattern, the order of heavier and lighter was set by drawing from a shuffled pack of playing cards. Jastrow did not know which way the difference ran. Published in 1885, this is often cited as the first experiment in psychology with deliberate random assignment and blinding, decades before Ronald Fisher made randomisation standard. They found people guessed above chance even when they felt they were guessing.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Randomisation and blinding were born in a psychology lab, not a hospital.
spotlights.memory_hook: A deck of cards was the first fair-test machine in psychology.

spotlights.name: The p-value and the magic 0.05
spotlights.spot_it: A number between 0 and 1, with 'p < .05' printed beside a result as if it were a stamp of truth.
spotlights.story_md: In his 1925 textbook, the statistician Ronald Fisher suggested that a result which chance would produce only one time in twenty was worth taking seriously, and that the 5% line was 'convenient'. He meant it as a signal to look further. Generations of journals turned it into a gate: below .05, publishable; above it, a failure. A p-value answers a narrow question: if there were no real effect, how often would data this extreme appear? It does not tell you the chance that the hypothesis is true, nor how big or important the effect is. In 2016 the American Statistical Association issued its first-ever statement on a statistical practice to say exactly this.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Treating 0.05 as a pass mark gave researchers a target to aim at, and aim they did.
spotlights.memory_hook: p is the chance of the data if nothing is going on, not the chance you are right.

spotlights.name: Effect size: how big, not just whether
spotlights.spot_it: Cohen's d: the gap between two group averages measured in standard deviations, with 0.2 small, 0.5 medium, 0.8 large.
spotlights.story_md: Jacob Cohen, a New York University psychologist, gave the field a common ruler. A d of 0.2 means the groups overlap almost completely: the average person in the treated group beats about 58% of the control group. A d of 0.8 means about 79%. Height difference between 15- and 16-year-old girls is small; between 13- and 18-year-olds is large. The replication projects found many published psychology effects that looked medium or large shrank to small or zero when repeated with big samples. A huge effect from a tiny, cheap manipulation is a warning sign: the world rarely works that way.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Knowing the size lets you judge whether a finding matters and whether it is plausible.
spotlights.memory_hook: Significant tells you 'probably not zero'. Effect size tells you 'so what'.

spotlights.name: Statistical power and the tiny sample
spotlights.spot_it: Studies with 15 to 30 people per group, chasing effects that would need hundreds.
spotlights.story_md: Power is the chance that a study will detect an effect that is really there. In 1962 Jacob Cohen checked a year of papers in the Journal of Abnormal and Social Psychology and found the average chance of detecting a medium-sized effect was about 0.48: a coin flip. Decades later, surveys found power had barely improved. Low power does two kinds of damage. Real effects get missed. Worse, among the small studies that do reach significance, many are flukes, and the real ones are exaggerated, because only the lucky high estimates cross the line. To reliably detect a small effect (d = 0.2) at the usual standard, you need about 400 people per group.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Underpowered studies fill journals with inflated and false results.
spotlights.memory_hook: A small study that 'works' is a lucky one, and luck does not replicate.

sections.title: Where experimental psychology came from
sections.intro_md:
Psychology began as a branch of philosophy and became a laboratory science in the late 19th century, in Germany. The founders were obsessed with measurement: reaction times in thousandths of a second, the smallest weight difference a hand can feel, how many nonsense syllables survive a day in memory.

From the start, the field also discovered how easily an experiment fools the experimenter. A horse in Berlin that seemed to do arithmetic, and a factory in Illinois where productivity seemed to rise whatever the managers changed, became the two great cautionary tales. Both are still taught, and one of them is now itself a partly mythical story.

A useful thread to follow: the oldest, simplest findings, measured on the researcher's own memory or senses with endless repetitions, have often replicated best. The flashy social findings of the 1990s and 2000s have done worst.

spotlights.name: Wilhelm Wundt's Leipzig laboratory
spotlights.spot_it: A bearded professor and his students around brass timing machines, measuring thought in milliseconds.
spotlights.story_md: In 1879 Wilhelm Wundt set aside a room at the University of Leipzig for psychological experiments, the date usually given for the birth of experimental psychology. His students timed how long it took to react to a light or a sound, and how much longer when they had to choose between responses, using a precision clock called the Hipp chronoscope. Wundt trained a large share of the next generation, including many of the first American psychology professors. His method relied on trained observers describing their own experience, which later psychologists rejected as unreliable. But the idea that the mind could be put on a lab bench and measured began here.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It made psychology an experimental science.
spotlights.memory_hook: Psychology's birth certificate is a stopwatch in Leipzig, 1879.

spotlights.name: Ebbinghaus and the forgetting curve
spotlights.spot_it: One man, thousands of nonsense syllables like 'DAX' and 'BOK', and a curve that drops steeply then levels off.
spotlights.story_md: Hermann Ebbinghaus was his own only subject. He memorised lists of meaningless syllables until he could recite them perfectly, then measured how much time he saved relearning them hours or days later. He found forgetting is fastest in the first hour and then slows. In 2015 two Amsterdam researchers, Jaap Murre and Joeri Dros, repeated the study on one subject, about 70 hours of learning and relearning. The curve came back, closely matching the 1880 original, including a small bump at 24 hours that they linked to sleep. A single-subject study from 130 years earlier replicated better than many modern experiments with hundreds of participants.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Careful measurement with many repetitions beats a big flashy sample.
spotlights.memory_hook: One man, nonsense syllables, and a curve that still holds 130 years later.

spotlights.name: Clever Hans, the horse that read people
spotlights.spot_it: A horse in a Berlin courtyard tapping out answers with his hoof, his owner beside him.
spotlights.story_md: Hans, a horse owned by a retired teacher, Wilhelm von Osten, seemed to add, subtract and tell the time by tapping. A commission of experts found no trick in 1904. Then the psychologist Oskar Pfungst tested him properly. When the questioner did not know the answer, or stood out of sight, Hans failed. He was watching tiny, unconscious movements of the questioner's head and body as the count reached the right number. Even Pfungst, knowing this, could not stop himself giving the cues. The 'Clever Hans effect' is why good experiments keep the person running them blind to the conditions.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It showed that experimenters can create the result they expect without meaning to.
spotlights.memory_hook: The horse could not count, but he could read your face.

spotlights.name: The Hawthorne effect, and its shaky origin
spotlights.spot_it: A Chicago-area telephone factory where workers supposedly worked harder whenever the lights changed.
spotlights.story_md: At Western Electric's Hawthorne Works near Chicago, researchers varied lighting to see how it affected output. The legend says productivity rose whether lights went up or down, because workers knew they were being watched. That became the 'Hawthorne effect'. When the economists Steven Levitt and John List found the original illumination data, long thought lost, and reanalysed it in 2011, the pattern was much weaker than the story: changes were mostly explained by Monday effects and the timing of experiments. Being observed can change behaviour, but the founding case for the idea is thinner than textbooks claimed.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Even psychology's cautionary tales need fact-checking.
spotlights.memory_hook: The famous lights study was dimmer than its legend.

sections.title: The textbook classics, looked at again
sections.intro_md:
Every introductory psychology course teaches a handful of dramatic studies. People shocking a stranger because a man in a lab coat told them to. Students turning cruel as prison guards. A child staring at a marshmallow. Healthy people admitted to psychiatric hospitals.

These studies shaped how the public thinks about human nature. They also came from an era with small samples, little oversight and no requirement to share data. Since 2010, historians have opened the archives, and replicators have rerun what ethics allows. The results split in an instructive way. Simple effects measured in many people, like conformity in a line-judging task, have held up. Grand stories built on one dramatic study, often with the method only half reported, have cracked.

The verdict on each is below. Read them as 'what we now know', not as debunking for sport.

spotlights.name: Milgram's obedience experiments
spotlights.spot_it: A volunteer at a fake shock generator with switches labelled up to 450 volts, a man in a grey coat saying 'please continue'.
spotlights.story_md: Stanley Milgram told volunteers they were helping study learning. Each time a 'learner' in the next room, an actor, got an answer wrong, they pressed a switch for a stronger shock. In the best-known version, 26 of 40 men, 65%, went all the way to 450 volts. The psychologist Gina Perry's study of the archives (2012) found Milgram ran more than 20 variations, with full obedience ranging from near zero to over 90%, and that many participants doubted the shocks were real. Jerry Burger's partial replication in 2009 stopped at 150 volts for ethical reasons; 70% were willing to go past that point, similar to Milgram's rate.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Obedience to authority is real, but more variable and conditional than the headline number.
spotlights.memory_hook: 65% was one version among more than twenty.

spotlights.name: The Stanford prison experiment
spotlights.spot_it: Students in smocks and stocking caps, guards in mirrored sunglasses, in a mock prison in a university basement.
spotlights.story_md: Philip Zimbardo put 24 male students in a fake prison in the basement of Stanford's psychology building, half as guards, half as prisoners. He stopped it after six days instead of 14, saying the guards had become abusive. For decades it was taught as proof that situations turn ordinary people cruel. In 2018 and 2019 the French researcher Thibault Le Texier, working from Stanford's archive, showed the guards were told what was expected of them and coached to be tough, and a recording has a staff member pushing a reluctant guard. The BBC Prison Study of 2002 found guards did not spontaneously turn tyrannical.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is now a lesson in demand characteristics, not in human nature.
spotlights.memory_hook: The guards were not just drunk on power; they were given a script.

spotlights.name: Asch's lines
spotlights.spot_it: One real participant among actors, all saying out loud which of three lines matches a target line, and the actors deliberately wrong.
spotlights.story_md: Solomon Asch showed a card with a line and three comparison lines. The answer was obvious; alone, people erred less than 1% of the time. But when seven actors gave the same wrong answer first, real participants went along on about a third of trials, and three in four conformed at least once. Asch himself stressed the other side: most answers were independent. A 1996 meta-analysis by Rod Bond and Peter Smith of 133 studies in 17 countries found conformity was higher in collectivist societies and had declined in the United States since the 1950s. The basic effect keeps coming back.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Social pressure bends even judgments of plain fact, though most people resist most of the time.
spotlights.memory_hook: Three lines, seven liars, one in three answers bent.

spotlights.name: The marshmallow test
spotlights.spot_it: A preschooler alone at a table with one treat, told they can have two if they wait.
spotlights.story_md: Walter Mischel's team at Stanford's Bing Nursery School let children choose: one small treat now, or two if they waited, up to 15 or 20 minutes, alone. Follow-ups in 1988 and 1990 reported that longer waiters later had better SAT scores, which made the test famous as a measure of self-control. But the follow-up samples were small, a few dozen to around a hundred children of Stanford staff and students. In 2018 Tyler Watts, Greg Duncan and Haonan Quan used a US study of more than 900 children from diverse backgrounds. The link with later achievement was about half the size, and shrank to near zero once family background and early ability were taken into account.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Waiting for a treat partly reflects a child's circumstances, not just willpower.
spotlights.memory_hook: The marshmallow measured the household as much as the child.

spotlights.name: On being sane in insane places
spotlights.spot_it: Eight healthy people claiming to hear a voice say 'thud', admitted to psychiatric hospitals.
spotlights.story_md: David Rosenhan reported in Science that he and seven others had got themselves admitted to 12 US hospitals by saying they heard voices saying 'empty', 'hollow' and 'thud'. Once inside they acted normally, yet stayed an average of 19 days and were discharged mostly with 'schizophrenia in remission'. The paper helped reshape American psychiatric diagnosis. The journalist Susannah Cahalan spent years on Rosenhan's papers for her 2019 book 'The Great Pretender'. She could identify only one other pseudopatient, found that Rosenhan's own medical record contradicted his account, and found one excluded participant whose positive experience did not fit the story. Many now think parts of the study were exaggerated or invented.
spotlights.why_it_matters: A paper that changed psychiatry may not have happened the way it was reported.
spotlights.memory_hook: Thud: the sound of a classic study falling over.

sections.title: The effects that faded
sections.intro_md:
Some findings did more than appear in textbooks. They became TED talks, airport bestsellers, corporate training and school policy. Strike a pose before an interview. Willpower is a muscle that runs out. Smile and you will feel happier. Classical music makes babies smarter.

Each rested on real, published experiments. Each then met large, preregistered replications run by many labs at once, where nobody could tweak the analysis after seeing the data. The pattern was similar every time: the effect shrank to small, or to nothing, or survived only in a narrower form.

The chart compares original and replication effect sizes in the big projects. When a finding is selected because it crossed a threshold, its first estimate is almost always too high. Statisticians call this the **winner's curse**, and it is one reason the second measurement of anything tends to be smaller than the first.

spotlights.name: Power posing
spotlights.spot_it: Hands on hips, feet apart, chin up: the 'Wonder Woman' pose held for two minutes before a stressful task.
spotlights.story_md: In 2010 Dana Carney, Amy Cuddy and Andy Yap reported that 42 people who held expansive poses for two minutes felt more powerful, took more risks, had higher testosterone and lower cortisol. Cuddy's 2012 TED talk became one of the most watched ever, with tens of millions of views. In 2015 Eva Ranehill's team tested 200 people and found no hormone or risk effects, only a small boost in feeling powerful. In 2016 Carney, the first author, posted a statement: 'I do not believe that power pose effects are real.' Cuddy argues that the effect on feelings of power is still supported. That narrower claim is what remains.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It became the public face of the crisis, and showed how a fragile finding can travel faster than its correction.
spotlights.memory_hook: The pose may make you feel taller. It does not change your hormones.

spotlights.name: Ego depletion: the radish study
spotlights.spot_it: Hungry students in a room smelling of fresh cookies, told to eat only the radishes.
spotlights.story_md: Roy Baumeister's 1998 experiment had students resist warm chocolate chip cookies and eat radishes instead. Afterwards they gave up on an unsolvable puzzle sooner, after about 8 minutes, compared with about 19 for those allowed cookies. Willpower, the theory said, is a limited resource that runs down like a battery. Hundreds of studies followed, and a 2010 meta-analysis put the effect at a medium-to-large d = 0.62. Then a 23-lab preregistered replication with 2,141 people (2016) found d = 0.04. A second, 36-lab test designed with Baumeister's colleague Kathleen Vohs (2021), with 3,531 people, found d = 0.06: the data were about four times more likely under no effect.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Hundreds of published studies can rest on an effect that may not exist.
spotlights.memory_hook: The radishes won: willpower did not visibly run out.

spotlights.name: The pen in the mouth
spotlights.spot_it: People holding a pen in their teeth (forcing a smile) or in their lips (blocking one) while rating cartoons.
spotlights.story_md: Fritz Strack's 1988 study found people holding a pen in their teeth rated Far Side cartoons as funnier than people holding it in their lips. It was a neat test of the idea that facial expressions feed back into feelings, without telling people to smile. In 2016, 17 labs and nearly 1,900 participants found no effect. Strack pointed out that the replications filmed participants, which might have made them self-conscious; a 2018 study suggested the effect appeared without cameras. In 2022 the Many Smiles Collaboration, with about 3,900 people in 19 countries, found that posed smiles produced small increases in happiness, but the pen method itself showed little.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It shows how a 'failed replication' can lead to a sharper, smaller truth rather than a simple no.
spotlights.memory_hook: Smiling may lift your mood a little. Chewing a pen does not.

spotlights.name: Walking slowly after reading 'Florida'
spotlights.spot_it: Students timed walking down a corridor after unscrambling sentences with words like 'wrinkle', 'bingo' and 'Florida'.
spotlights.story_md: John Bargh's 1996 study reported that students primed with words about old age walked down a hallway more slowly, by about a second over 9.75 metres. It became a symbol of 'social priming', the idea that subtle cues steer behaviour unawares. In 2012 Stéphane Doyen's team in Brussels repeated it with infrared sensors instead of a stopwatch. No effect. Then the twist: when they told the experimenters to expect slower walking and let them time it by hand, the slowing appeared. The likely explanation was the experimenters, not the words. Bargh strongly disputed the replication. It was the episode that prompted Kahneman's 'train wreck' letter.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It showed how unblinded experimenters can produce the effect they expect.
spotlights.memory_hook: Clever Hans came back, wearing a lab coat and holding a stopwatch.

spotlights.name: The Mozart effect
spotlights.spot_it: College students listening to a Mozart piano sonata for 10 minutes before a paper-folding puzzle.
spotlights.story_md: In 1993 Frances Rauscher and colleagues reported in Nature that 36 students did better on a spatial reasoning task after 10 minutes of Mozart's Sonata for Two Pianos in D major, an effect that lasted about 10 to 15 minutes. The press turned it into 'Mozart makes you smarter'. In 1998 the governor of Georgia proposed sending every newborn a classical music CD. A 1999 meta-analysis by Christopher Chabris found a tiny effect, and a 2010 meta-analysis of about 3,000 people concluded there was little evidence for a specific Mozart effect. Any short-lived boost seems to come from enjoyment and arousal, from any music you like.
spotlights.why_it_matters: A small, short lab effect turned into public policy for babies.
spotlights.memory_hook: Mozart did not raise IQs; he raised moods, and so does any music you like.

sections.title: How honest scientists fooled themselves
sections.intro_md:
Most of the crisis was not fraud. It was a system that rewarded ordinary people for producing exciting results, plus statistical habits that made exciting results easy to produce by accident.

Think of a researcher with a promising idea, a small budget and a career that depends on publishing in good journals. Journals strongly prefer positive, novel findings. A study that 'did not work' goes in a drawer. One that worked after the third way of analysing it gets written up as if that analysis was the plan all along. Nobody feels like they are cheating. Each step seems reasonable.

In 2012 Leslie John, George Loewenstein and Drazen Prelec surveyed about 2,000 US psychologists, with incentives for honesty. Large shares admitted to at least one questionable practice, like failing to report all measures or deciding to collect more data after looking at the results. A 2010 analysis by Daniele Fanelli found that psychology and psychiatry papers reported positive results more often than any other field.

spotlights.name: p-hacking and the garden of forking paths
spotlights.spot_it: Trying analysis after analysis until one crosses p < .05, then reporting that one.
spotlights.story_md: Flip a fair coin enough times and you will get a run of heads. Analyse data enough ways and something will be 'significant'. Simmons, Nelson and Simonsohn showed that four choices, like which of two measures to report or whether to add 10 more people, could take the false positive rate from 5% to 61%. The statistician Andrew Gelman added a subtler point he called the 'garden of forking paths': you do not even have to try many analyses. If the choices would have been different had the data looked different, the p-value is already misleading. The fix is to decide the analysis before seeing the data.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It explains how many false findings came from honest researchers.
spotlights.memory_hook: Torture the data long enough and it will confess to anything.

spotlights.name: HARKing: hypothesising after the results are known
spotlights.spot_it: A paper whose introduction predicts exactly the surprising result found, because it was written after the result.
spotlights.story_md: The social psychologist Norbert Kerr gave this habit its name in 1998. You run a study, find something unexpected, then write the paper as if you had predicted it. A popular 1980s guide for young psychologists, by Daryl Bem, openly advised authors to write 'the article that makes the most sense now that you have seen the results'. The trouble is that a hypothesis chosen after looking at the data is not tested by those data. It is a description of them. The same noise that produced the pattern will not repeat in the next sample.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It disguises exploration as confirmation.
spotlights.memory_hook: Drawing the target around the arrow after it lands.

spotlights.name: The file drawer problem
spotlights.spot_it: Journals filled with the 5% of chance successes while the 95% of null results stay in filing cabinets.
spotlights.story_md: Robert Rosenthal named it in 1979: if journals publish mainly significant results, the literature becomes a collection of lucky draws. Imagine 20 labs test a useless idea. One gets p < .05 by chance and publishes. Nineteen file their results away. Readers see one study, all positive. Publication bias can be detected with a 'funnel plot', which plots each study's result against its size. Without bias, small studies scatter evenly around the truth. With bias, one corner of the funnel is missing: the small studies that found nothing. Meta-analyses of ego depletion and power posing both showed this lopsided shape.
spotlights.why_it_matters: What does not get published shapes what we believe as much as what does.
spotlights.memory_hook: For every published success, count the drawers you cannot see.

spotlights.name: WEIRD people
spotlights.spot_it: Western, Educated, Industrialised, Rich, Democratic: the narrow slice of humanity in most psychology studies.
spotlights.story_md: In 2010 Joseph Henrich, Steven Heine and Ara Norenzayan reported that 96% of subjects in top psychology journals (2003 to 2007) came from Western industrialised countries with about 12% of the world's population, and 68% from the United States alone. A random American undergraduate was about 4,000 times more likely to be a research subject than a random person outside the West. Some 'universal' findings turned out to vary. The Müller-Lyer illusion, two lines that look different lengths because of arrow-shaped ends, is much weaker for San foragers in the Kalahari than for students in the United States. Replication within one culture says nothing about the rest.
spotlights.why_it_matters: A finding can replicate perfectly and still not describe most humans.
spotlights.memory_hook: Psychology studied the world's weirdest people and called it human nature.

spotlights.name: Why surprising plus small means suspicious
spotlights.spot_it: A cheap manipulation, a big effect, a sample of 40, and a press release.
spotlights.story_md: John Ioannidis's 2005 essay 'Why Most Published Research Findings Are False' used simple arithmetic. A finding is less likely to be true when studies are small, effects are small, many relationships are tested, designs are flexible, there are financial or prestige interests, and the field is hot with many teams chasing significance. Social priming studies of the 2000s ticked nearly every box. It became the most-read paper PLOS Medicine had published. The 2015 replication data fitted his logic: original studies with the smallest p-values and the least surprising claims were the most likely to replicate.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It gave a checklist for predicting which findings will fail.
spotlights.memory_hook: The more surprising the claim and the smaller the study, the bigger the doubt.

sections.title: When it was fraud
sections.intro_md:
Fraud is a small part of the replication story, but it is the part people remember. Making up data is rare; a 2009 meta-analysis of surveys found about 2% of scientists admit fabricating or falsifying data at least once. Yet a handful of cases did outsized damage because the fabricators were stars, their findings were cited thousands of times, and their results fed policy and business.

What is striking is who caught them. Not journals, and rarely universities. Mostly it was junior colleagues, graduate students, and a small group of volunteer data detectives who downloaded public datasets and noticed numbers that were too neat, impossible means, or Excel rows sorted in suspicious ways.

The cases below span 50 years. Note the difference between outright fabrication (Stapel), misconduct ruled by a university (Hauser, Wansink, Gino) and findings retracted because data were shown to be fake while the author denied faking them (Ariely). Some of these cases are still in court.

spotlights.name: Diederik Stapel, the data inventor
spotlights.spot_it: A Dutch social psychologist who handed students finished datasets, never letting them see the schools where 'data' were collected.
spotlights.story_md: Stapel was dean of social and behavioural sciences at Tilburg University and a media favourite, with studies such as one claiming that messy train stations made white commuters more prejudiced. He designed studies with students, then said he would collect the data himself at schools he knew, and returned with perfect results. Three junior researchers noticed patterns too good to be real and reported him in August 2011. An investigation found fraud in 55 of his papers and 10 PhD theses he supervised. He has 58 retractions. He confessed, wrote a memoir titled 'Ontsporing' ('Derailment'), and returned his PhD.
spotlights.why_it_matters: He showed how a system without data sharing could be gamed for years.
spotlights.memory_hook: Too good to be true was literally true: he made it up.

spotlights.name: Cyril Burt's twins
spotlights.spot_it: A British psychologist whose twin studies reported the same correlation to three decimal places as his sample grew.
spotlights.story_md: Cyril Burt was the most influential British educational psychologist of his time, and his studies of identical twins raised apart supported the idea that intelligence is largely inherited. That work fed into the 11-plus exam that sorted British children into schools. After his death in 1971, critics noticed that his reported correlation of 0.771 stayed identical to three decimal places as the number of twins changed, a near-impossibility. Two co-authors could not be found. His official biographer concluded in 1979 that he had committed fraud, a verdict some later writers have contested. The case remains disputed, but the suspicious numbers are not.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Numbers that never move as samples grow are a red flag.
spotlights.memory_hook: 0.771, 0.771, 0.771: real data are never that loyal.

spotlights.name: Brian Wansink and the bottomless soup bowl
spotlights.spot_it: A Cornell food scientist famous for the self-refilling soup bowl and the advice to use smaller plates.
spotlights.story_md: Wansink ran Cornell's Food and Brand Lab. His studies found people ate 73% more soup from a bowl secretly refilled through a tube under the table, and that smaller plates helped people eat less. They earned him an Ig Nobel Prize in 2007 and shaped US school lunch policy. In 2016 he blogged praise for a visiting student who had dug through a 'failed' dataset until she found publishable results. Readers recognised p-hacking and began checking his papers, finding impossible numbers. Cornell found academic misconduct in 2018. He has more than a dozen retractions and left Cornell in 2019.
spotlights.why_it_matters: He undid himself by describing p-hacking proudly on his own blog.
spotlights.memory_hook: The soup bowl never emptied, and neither did the errors.

spotlights.name: The honesty study with dishonest data
spotlights.spot_it: A paper showing that signing an honesty pledge at the top of a form made people more honest, built on a fabricated car-insurance dataset.
spotlights.story_md: In 2012 Lisa Shu, Nina Mazar, Francesca Gino, Dan Ariely and Max Bazerman reported in PNAS that customers who signed at the top of an insurance form reported about 10% more miles driven than those who signed at the bottom. In August 2021 the Data Colada blog showed the mileage numbers were uniformly distributed, as if generated by a random number function, and that half the dataset appeared copied with small random additions in a different font. The insurer, The Hartford, said it had given Ariely data on about 3,700 policies, not the more than 13,000 in the paper. The paper was retracted. Ariely said he did not fabricate the data and did not know who did.
spotlights.why_it_matters: A study about honesty became the clearest lesson in why raw data must be shared.
spotlights.memory_hook: The numbers on honesty were themselves a lie.

spotlights.name: Francesca Gino and the end of tenure
spotlights.spot_it: A Harvard Business School professor of honesty and ethics, placed on leave in 2023 and stripped of tenure in May 2025.
spotlights.story_md: In June 2023 Data Colada published posts on four papers co-authored by Gino, a star researcher on dishonesty, showing signs of data tampering, including rows that appeared out of order in a sorted spreadsheet. A Harvard committee, helped by an outside forensic firm, concluded she had committed research misconduct. Harvard put her on unpaid leave in 2023 and revoked her tenure in May 2025, reported as the first such revocation at Harvard in decades. Gino denies fabricating data. She sued Harvard and the Data Colada authors for 25 million dollars; the claims against the bloggers were dismissed in 2024. Her suit against Harvard, and Harvard's countersuit, were still running in late 2026.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It showed universities can impose the heaviest penalty, and that it takes years.
spotlights.memory_hook: A professor of honesty lost the job that is meant to be permanent.

spotlights.name: Data Colada and the data detectives
spotlights.spot_it: Three behavioural scientists who check other people's spreadsheets, and a growing band of volunteer sleuths with tools like GRIM.
spotlights.story_md: Uri Simonsohn, Leif Nelson and Joseph Simmons, the authors of the Beatles study, started the Data Colada blog in 2013. Simonsohn had already exposed two psychologists in 2012 by spotting results too consistent to come from real samples. Other sleuths built simple checks. Nick Brown and James Heathers's GRIM test (2016) asks whether a reported average is even possible: with 20 people answering in whole numbers, a mean of 3.47 cannot exist, because the possible means go in steps of 0.05. Applied to 71 papers, it found that about half reported at least one impossible mean. Most were errors, but some led to retractions.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Outsiders with open data and arithmetic now police the literature.
spotlights.memory_hook: Twenty people cannot average 3.47: arithmetic catches what peer review misses.

sections.title: The repair kit
sections.intro_md:
The good news of this story is how fast psychology changed. Within a decade of 2011 it went from the field with the worst reputation for replication to the one that led the reform movement across science.

The core idea is simple: separate the decisions from the data. Write down your hypothesis, sample size and analysis before you collect anything, put that plan somewhere with a timestamp, and share your raw data afterwards. If you then explore and find something unexpected, label it as exploration.

Around that idea grew infrastructure: a free platform for registering plans and sharing data, a new kind of journal article accepted before results exist, giant collaborations that run the same study in dozens of countries, badges that reward openness, and prediction markets that bet on which findings will survive. None of this guarantees truth. But it makes errors visible faster, and it makes 'we found nothing' publishable.

spotlights.name: Preregistration
spotlights.spot_it: A time-stamped plan, written before data collection, saying exactly what will be tested and how.
spotlights.story_md: Medicine has required trial registration since the 2000s, after drug companies were caught hiding unflattering results. Psychology borrowed the idea. On a site such as the Open Science Framework, a researcher writes the hypothesis, the number of participants, the exclusion rules and the exact statistical test, then freezes it. Readers can check whether the paper matches the plan. Studies of the effect are striking: in a 2021 analysis by Anne Scheel and colleagues, 96% of standard psychology papers reported support for their first hypothesis, compared with 44% of Registered Reports. Preregistration is not a cage; you can still explore. You just have to say so.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It makes p-hacking and HARKing visible.
spotlights.memory_hook: Call your shot before you take it.

spotlights.name: Registered Reports
spotlights.spot_it: A journal article accepted for publication on the strength of its question and method, before any results exist.
spotlights.story_md: The Cardiff neuroscientist Chris Chambers launched Registered Reports at the journal Cortex in 2013. Authors submit their introduction and methods. Reviewers judge whether the question matters and the design is sound. If accepted, the journal promises to publish whatever the results, as long as the authors follow the plan. That removes the incentive to massage data, because a null result is as publishable as a positive one. More than 300 journals now offer the format. The striking result of the Scheel analysis, 44% positive against 96%, suggests what the normal literature would look like if negative results were not hidden.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It judges research by its question and design, not its outcome.
spotlights.memory_hook: Accepted before the answer is known, so the answer does not have to please.

spotlights.name: The Center for Open Science
spotlights.spot_it: A non-profit in Charlottesville, Virginia that runs the free Open Science Framework.
spotlights.story_md: Brian Nosek and Jeffrey Spies founded the Center for Open Science in 2013 with money from the Laura and John Arnold Foundation. It built the Open Science Framework, a free platform where researchers store plans, materials and data. It also coordinated the Reproducibility Projects in psychology and cancer biology, and was a lead partner in SCORE, the effort funded by the US defence research agency DARPA to see whether replicability can be predicted. Its 'TOP guidelines' rate journals on transparency. By the 2020s, preregistration and data-sharing badges were routine at many psychology journals, largely through this one organisation's lobbying and tools.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It turned reform ideas into free, everyday tools.
spotlights.memory_hook: A non-profit built the filing cabinet that anyone can open.

spotlights.name: Betting on replication
spotlights.spot_it: Researchers trading 'shares' that pay out if a study replicates.
spotlights.story_md: In 2015 Anna Dreber and colleagues set up prediction markets where psychologists bet on which of the Reproducibility Project's studies would replicate. The market prices predicted outcomes correctly 71% of the time, better than a simple survey of the same people. Later projects found similar accuracy. Experts, it turned out, could smell which findings were weak: surprising, small, with p-values just under .05. The 2026 SCORE results found the best human forecasting methods were about 75% accurate, and that AI models matched the broad patterns but were worse at telling individual claims apart. If informed bets can predict failure, the warning signs are visible in advance.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Researchers' collective judgement about which findings are fragile is fairly accurate.
spotlights.memory_hook: The market knew which studies were bluffing.

sections.title: What held up
sections.intro_md:
It would be a bad lesson to leave today thinking psychology is mostly junk. Many findings are among the best-replicated in all of science, demonstrated thousands of times in classrooms, across cultures and in large, preregistered tests.

The robust ones tend to share features. The effect is big relative to noise. It is measured many times within each person, not once. The manipulation is direct, not a subtle prime. And the theory makes a specific prediction that could easily have failed.

These are also the findings most worth knowing for daily life. How you study, how numbers anchor your judgments, how personality predicts outcomes, and how people really behave in a crisis are all on solid ground.

spotlights.name: The Stroop effect
spotlights.spot_it: The word RED printed in green ink, and you are asked to name the ink colour.
spotlights.story_md: John Ridley Stroop, an American psychologist who later spent his life teaching the Bible at a Tennessee college, published his PhD experiment in 1935. People took about 74% longer to name ink colours when the colours spelled conflicting colour words than when they named plain colour patches. Reading is so automatic you cannot switch it off. The effect has been replicated in thousands of studies, in dozens of languages, in children and adults, and is now a standard test in neuropsychology. It is among the most cited experiments in the history of psychology, and you can demonstrate it at your dining table in a minute.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is a model of a robust effect: large, immediate, repeatable by anyone.
spotlights.memory_hook: Your brain reads the word before it sees the colour.

spotlights.name: The testing effect
spotlights.spot_it: Students who quiz themselves remember more a week later than students who reread.
spotlights.story_md: Henry Roediger and Jeffrey Karpicke had students read prose passages, then either reread them or take recall tests. After five minutes, rereaders did slightly better. After a week, the testing group remembered far more, about 56% against 42% in one experiment. Retrieval practice has replicated in hundreds of studies, in classrooms, with medical students and children, in different subjects and countries. It is why this app gives you flashcards and quizzes rather than just text. Pair it with spacing, reviewing at growing intervals, another of the most robust findings in memory research, going back to Ebbinghaus.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Pulling information out of memory strengthens it more than putting it in again.
spotlights.memory_hook: Testing is not just measuring learning; it is learning.

spotlights.name: Anchoring
spotlights.spot_it: A random number, from a wheel or the last digits of your phone, dragging your next estimate towards it.
spotlights.story_md: Amos Tversky and Daniel Kahneman rigged a wheel of fortune to stop at 10 or 65, then asked people what percentage of United Nations member countries were African. Those who saw 10 guessed 25% on average; those who saw 65 guessed 45%. An obviously irrelevant number moved their answer. In Many Labs 1 (2014), anchoring questions, such as the height of Mount Everest after a high or low anchor, produced some of the largest effects of all 13 tested, replicating in every sample. Anchoring shows up in salary negotiations, house prices, sentencing and 'was 1,999, now 999' price tags.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Robust biases are the ones worth guarding against in your own decisions.
spotlights.memory_hook: The first number in the room wins, even if it came from a spinning wheel.

spotlights.name: The Big Five personality traits
spotlights.spot_it: Openness, Conscientiousness, Extraversion, Agreeableness, Neuroticism: OCEAN.
spotlights.story_md: Personality psychologists describe people on five broad dimensions that show up in questionnaires in dozens of languages. In 2019 Christopher Soto tested 78 published links between the Big Five and life outcomes, such as conscientiousness predicting job performance or neuroticism predicting relationship trouble, in new samples totalling about 6,000 people. 87% replicated, with effects about 77% of the original size. The difference from social priming is instructive: personality research uses large samples, reliable measures and correlations measured many times, exactly the features that make results durable.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Not all of psychology is fragile; fields with big samples and good measures did well.
spotlights.memory_hook: OCEAN came through the storm with 87% of its findings afloat.

spotlights.name: Kitty Genovese, and what CCTV shows
spotlights.spot_it: A New York murder said to have been watched by 38 silent neighbours, and modern street cameras that tell a different story.
spotlights.story_md: On 13 March 1964 Kitty Genovese was killed in Kew Gardens, Queens. A New York Times story said 38 witnesses watched and did nothing. The story inspired research on the 'bystander effect', the finding that people are less likely to help when others are present, which holds up in lab meta-analyses. But the 38 figure was wrong: few saw the attack, it was partly out of sight, at least one neighbour called police, and a neighbour held her as she died. In 2020 Richard Philpot and colleagues analysed 219 CCTV recordings of street fights in Lancaster, Amsterdam and Cape Town. In nine of ten, at least one bystander intervened, and more bystanders meant more help.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The lab effect is real, but the real world is kinder than the legend.
spotlights.memory_hook: Thirty-eight silent witnesses was a myth; nine in ten fights draw a helper.

sections.title: The India connection
sections.intro_md:
India enters this story three ways.

First, as a missing population. Indians are about one in six people on Earth but a tiny share of subjects in the studies that built psychology's textbooks. When researchers do test findings here, results sometimes differ, and large multi-country collaborations have started including Indian labs.

Second, as the site of some of the most influential field experiments in behavioural science. Rural Uttar Pradesh and Tamil Nadu produced landmark studies on caste identity and on how poverty affects thinking. India is also the biggest home of the randomised field trial in development economics, the approach that won Abhijit Banerjee, Esther Duflo and Michael Kremer the 2019 Nobel prize.

Third, as a research system with its own integrity crisis. Indian science has grown fast, and with it retractions, paper mills and predatory journals. A 2025 index of research-integrity risk put nine Indian universities in its global top ten.

spotlights.name: Narendra Nath Sen Gupta and the Calcutta lab
spotlights.spot_it: A Harvard-trained philosopher who set up India's first experimental psychology laboratory in Calcutta.
spotlights.story_md: Narendra Nath Sen Gupta studied at Harvard under Hugo Münsterberg, himself a student of Wundt. Back in India he founded the psychology laboratory at the University of Calcutta in 1915, and in 1916 the country's first independent Department of Experimental Psychology. He later founded the Indian Psychological Association and edited the Indian Journal of Psychology. Calcutta also produced Girindrasekhar Bose, who founded the Indian Psychoanalytical Society in 1922 and argued with Freud by letter. So India's first psychology was lab-based and Wundtian, measuring perception and reaction times, the same tradition whose simple measures replicate best today.
spotlights.why_it_matters: India's psychology began in the same lab tradition as Leipzig, only 36 years later.
spotlights.memory_hook: From Leipzig to Harvard to Calcutta: a two-step line of teachers to Wundt.

spotlights.name: Caste and the maze test
spotlights.spot_it: Boys from different castes solving paper mazes for money, with and without their caste being announced.
spotlights.story_md: World Bank economists Karla Hoff and Priyanka Pandey asked 642 junior high school boys in Uttar Pradesh villages, half high caste and half low caste, to solve mazes for cash per maze. When caste was not mentioned, there was no gap between the groups. When each boy's name, village and caste were read aloud before the task, low-caste boys' performance fell, opening a gap of about 25%. When rewards were made to depend partly on a random draw, the gap vanished. The authors concluded that low-caste boys expected to be judged unfairly when caste was visible. It is a field cousin of 'stereotype threat', whose lab evidence has itself replicated unevenly.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Identity cues can change performance, and this was shown with real stakes, not a lab survey.
spotlights.memory_hook: Say the caste out loud, and the mazes got harder.

spotlights.name: Poverty and thinking: Tamil Nadu sugarcane farmers
spotlights.spot_it: The same farmers tested on reasoning puzzles before harvest, when cash was short, and after, when they had been paid.
spotlights.story_md: Anandi Mani, Sendhil Mullainathan, Eldar Shafir and Jiaying Zhao studied sugarcane farmers in Tamil Nadu, who are paid once a year at harvest. Before harvest, when many had pawned belongings and taken loans, they scored worse on Raven's matrices and a Stroop-like task than the same farmers did after being paid. The authors argued that money worries consume mental bandwidth, an effect they compared to losing a night's sleep. The study became central to 'scarcity' theory and to policy talk about the poor. Later work questioned parts of the lab evidence, and a large replication of a related scarcity paper did not find the effect, so the size remains debated.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is a landmark Indian field study in psychology whose strength is still being tested.
spotlights.memory_hook: Before harvest, the mind is busy counting rupees.

spotlights.name: J-PAL and the randomised field trial in India
spotlights.spot_it: Randomised experiments run in Indian villages and schools, from Udaipur to Vadodara, testing what actually works.
spotlights.story_md: Abhijit Banerjee, Esther Duflo and Sendhil Mullainathan founded the Abdul Latif Jameel Poverty Action Lab at MIT in 2003. Many of its best-known trials ran in India: remedial tutoring by young women from the community in Vadodara and Mumbai schools; offering a kilogram of lentils to mothers in Udaipur district to raise child immunisation rates, which rose from 6% to 39% in villages with the incentive. These are psychology's methods, random assignment and preregistration, applied to policy. Banerjee, Duflo and Kremer won the 2019 Nobel prize in economics. Critics note that a result in one district may not transfer to another, which is the replication problem in a new form.
spotlights.why_it_matters: India became the world's laboratory for testing policies the way psychologists test claims.
spotlights.memory_hook: A kilo of lentils raised vaccination sixfold in Udaipur's trial villages.

spotlights.name: India's integrity problem in numbers
spotlights.spot_it: A ranking built on retractions and papers in delisted journals, with Indian universities crowding the top.
spotlights.story_md: Lokman Meho of the American University of Beirut built a Research Integrity Risk Index from two measures: retractions per 1,000 papers and the share of papers in journals delisted by Scopus or Web of Science. In the June 2025 release, nine of the ten highest-risk institutions in the world were Indian, led by Graphic Era University in Dehradun. Anna University in Chennai had 372 papers retracted from its 2022 and 2023 output. Retraction Watch counted 887 retractions from India in 2025, second only to China. The drivers differ from psychology's crisis: paper mills, citation cartels and pressure created by publication-count targets for jobs and rankings.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Incentives that reward counting papers produce papers, not knowledge.
spotlights.memory_hook: When the metric is paper count, the papers multiply and the truth does not.

sections.title: It was never just psychology
sections.intro_md:
Psychology got the headlines partly because it looked hardest at itself. When other fields ran the same kind of audit, many did no better, and some did worse.

Cancer biology, where failed replications mean wasted drug programmes, came out badly. Economics did somewhat better, partly because data-sharing rules came earlier. Neuroscience had the same low-power problem. Medicine had learned the hard way decades earlier, with trial registration forced on it by scandals over hidden drug data.

The common factors are the same everywhere: pressure to publish, journals that prize novelty, small samples, flexible analysis and no one checking. The common fixes are the same too. The lesson is not that one science is bad, but that any field that does not repeat its experiments will slowly fill with false findings.

spotlights.name: Amgen's 53 landmark cancer papers
spotlights.spot_it: A drug company's scientists trying to confirm the papers they planned to build medicines on, and mostly failing.
spotlights.story_md: Before investing in a new drug target, Amgen's scientists tried to confirm the original lab findings. In 2012 C. Glenn Begley, former head of cancer research there, and Lee Ellis reported in Nature that of 53 'landmark' papers, only 6, about 11%, could be confirmed. In some cases even the original authors could not repeat their own experiment. A year earlier Bayer had reported that only about a quarter of 67 in-house projects matched published data. Neither company published the list of papers, which drew criticism, but the numbers set off alarm across biomedicine.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It put a cost on irreproducibility: wasted years of drug development.
spotlights.memory_hook: Six of 53: the cancer papers that held when a drug company checked.

spotlights.name: Reproducibility Project: Cancer Biology
spotlights.spot_it: An eight-year attempt to repeat key experiments from 53 high-impact cancer papers.
spotlights.story_md: The Center for Open Science and Science Exchange planned to repeat 193 experiments from 53 widely cited cancer biology papers published between 2010 and 2012. They managed only 50 experiments from 23 papers. The rest were blocked because methods were too vague, materials were unavailable, or authors did not help: none of the 193 experiments was described in enough detail to repeat without asking the authors. Where replications ran, effect sizes were on median 85% smaller than the originals. Of the positive effects, 40% replicated on three or more of five criteria. The final reports, in eLife in December 2021, made opacity itself a finding.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It showed that in some fields you cannot even attempt a replication without the original authors' help.
spotlights.memory_hook: 193 experiments planned, 50 done, effects 85% smaller.

spotlights.name: The Brazilian Reproducibility Initiative
spotlights.spot_it: A whole country's biomedical labs checking a sample of their own national research.
spotlights.story_md: Instead of picking famous papers, Brazilian researchers led by Olavo Amaral sampled ordinary Brazilian biomedical studies using three common methods: a cell viability assay, a gene expression test (RT-PCR) and a mouse anxiety maze. Fifty-six labs ran 143 replications of 56 experiments. Depending on the criterion, between about 15% and 45% replicated, and the differences between groups were on median 58% smaller than in the originals. It was the first estimate of replicability for a national research system rather than a famous literature. The project won the Einstein Foundation's institutional award in 2025.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It showed the problem is not limited to famous papers in rich countries.
spotlights.memory_hook: Brazil checked itself and found the same shrinking effects.

spotlights.name: Economics: the spreadsheet that shaped austerity
spotlights.spot_it: A famous growth-and-debt paper whose Excel formula skipped five countries.
spotlights.story_md: In 2010 Carmen Reinhart and Kenneth Rogoff reported that countries with public debt above 90% of GDP had sharply lower growth. Politicians in the US and Europe cited it to justify spending cuts. In 2013 Thomas Herndon, a 28-year-old graduate student at the University of Massachusetts Amherst, could not reproduce it for a class assignment. Using the authors' own spreadsheet, he found an Excel range that left out five countries, plus debatable weighting. Corrected, average growth above 90% debt was about 2.2%, not minus 0.1%. The authors accepted the coding error but defended their broader conclusion. A student homework exercise is now a textbook case for sharing data.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Reproducibility checks matter most where research drives policy.
spotlights.memory_hook: A graduate student's homework found five missing countries in one Excel formula.

sections.title: Myths and facts
sections.intro_md:
The replication crisis has generated its own myths, some from critics and some from defenders. Each one below is common, and each is wrong in a specific way.

The most important correction is about what a failed replication means. A single failed replication is evidence, not a verdict. The original might have been a fluke. The replication might have been badly done, underpowered, or run in a setting where the effect does not hold. What counts is the weight of evidence across many high-quality attempts. That is why the large, multi-lab, preregistered tests carry so much weight: they remove most of the excuses at once.

The second correction is about p-values, which almost everyone, including many researchers, has at some point misread.

spotlights.name: Myth: p = 0.05 means a 95% chance the finding is true
spotlights.spot_it: A researcher, a journalist or a textbook saying 'there is only a 5% chance this result is due to chance'.
spotlights.story_md: A p-value of .05 means: if there were truly no effect, results this extreme would turn up about 5% of the time. That is not the same as a 5% chance the effect is fake. The real chance depends on how plausible the idea was to begin with and how powerful the study was. If only one in ten tested ideas in a field is true and studies have 50% power, then roughly half of 'significant' findings at .05 are false. This is why 72 researchers in 2018 proposed moving the bar for new discoveries to .005, and why the American Statistical Association warned in 2016 against using .05 as a pass mark.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Misreading p-values made weak evidence look strong.
spotlights.memory_hook: p is about the data, not about whether you are right.

spotlights.name: Myth: the crisis means psychology is junk
spotlights.spot_it: Someone dismissing any psychology finding with 'that field does not replicate'.
spotlights.story_md: Replication rates of around 40 to 60% are bad, but they are not zero, and they are not uniform. Effects measured on large samples with good measures, like personality traits, memory and attention, did well. Many classic cognitive findings replicate near 100% in classroom demonstrations. The fragile results cluster in one style of research: single studies with small samples, subtle manipulations and big claims about behaviour. Psychology also did the most to expose its own problems. The fields that never checked are not necessarily more reliable; they are just less audited.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Knowing which findings are fragile is more useful than dismissing all of them.
spotlights.memory_hook: Not all psychology broke. The flashy, tiny-sample kind did.

sections.title: What is happening now
sections.intro_md:
Fifteen years after 2011, the replication crisis has moved from shock to routine maintenance, with occasional new shocks.

On 1 April 2026 the biggest audit yet landed in Nature: SCORE, a DARPA-funded project with 865 researchers, reported on reproducibility, robustness and replicability across the social and behavioural sciences. Its headline number, 49% of 164 papers replicated, sits close to earlier estimates, which suggests the problem was real and stable, not a quirk of one project.

Meanwhile the reformers have faced their own test. In September 2024 a high-profile paper arguing that rigorous methods yield highly replicable findings was itself retracted, for failing to follow its own preregistration. And the Gino case, which began in 2021 with a blog post, was still in court in autumn 2026. The fight is now less about whether there is a problem and more about who pays for checking, and how to keep scrutiny fair.

spotlights.name: SCORE: 3,900 claims, 865 researchers
spotlights.spot_it: A DARPA-funded audit of the social sciences, published as three Nature papers and six preprints.
spotlights.story_md: SCORE, Systematizing Confidence in Open Research and Evidence, asked whether the credibility of social science claims could be measured and predicted. Researchers sampled claims from about 3,900 papers. Reproduction tests on 143 papers found 74% reproduced at least approximately from the original data. Robustness tests on 100 papers found the conclusion held in 74% of reanalyses by other teams, with 2% reaching the opposite conclusion. Replication with new data on 164 papers found 49% succeeded, and replication effects (r = 0.10) were less than half the originals (r = 0.25). Rates ranged from about 43% to 63% by discipline, and were higher for papers in journals requiring data sharing.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is the largest and most recent estimate, and it confirms the earlier ones.
spotlights.memory_hook: Half again: 164 papers, 49% replicated, effects cut by more than half.

spotlights.name: The rigour paper that was retracted
spotlights.spot_it: A Nature Human Behaviour paper by leading reformers claiming 86% replication with best practices, then withdrawn.
spotlights.story_md: John Protzko, Brian Nosek, Jonathan Schooler and colleagues ran a 'prospective replication' study: four labs discovered 16 new effects using preregistration and large samples, then replicated each other's. They reported 86% replication with effects at 97% of the original size. Critics Joseph Bak-Coleman and Berna Devezer noticed that the headline claim was not in the preregistration and that analyses were chosen after seeing data. The journal retracted the paper on 24 September 2024, citing these issues. No one alleged fabrication. The irony was widely noted: the reformers were held to their own standard, and the system worked.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Openness means reformers' work gets checked too.
spotlights.memory_hook: The paper praising preregistration broke its own preregistration.

sections.title: How to read a psychology headline, and recap
sections.intro_md:
You now have the toolkit to judge a claim like 'a two-minute pose makes you more confident' or 'people who do X live longer'. Ask six questions.

1. **How many people?** Dozens is a pilot. Hundreds or thousands is evidence.
2. **Was it preregistered or a Registered Report?** If so, flexible analysis is much less likely.
3. **Has anyone else replicated it**, ideally in a big multi-lab test? One study is a rumour.
4. **How big is the effect?** 'Significant' only means probably not zero.
5. **Who were the subjects?** American undergraduates are not humanity.
6. **How surprising is it?** A tiny nudge with a huge effect on complex behaviour is a red flag. Extraordinary claims need extraordinary evidence.

The recap in one paragraph: psychology tests claims by random assignment, blinding and statistics. In 2011 it learned that common habits, p-hacking, HARKing, small samples and hiding null results, could make false findings routine. Big replication projects found roughly half of findings hold, usually weaker. Fraud was rare but damaging. The fixes, preregistration, Registered Reports, open data and many-lab studies, have spread across science. The robust core, memory, attention, anchoring, personality, remains, and is worth knowing.

cards.back: That hearing the song made people 1.5 years younger. It was a deliberate demonstration that common flexible analysis can prove the impossible.

cards.front: In Bem's curtain experiment, how often did students pick the curtain hiding an erotic picture?
cards.back: 53.1%, against 50% by chance.

cards.front: In 2012 Daniel Kahneman wrote to priming researchers: 'I see a ___ looming.'
cards.back: train wreck

cards.front: Reproducibility Project: Psychology (2015): what share of significant originals came back significant?
cards.back: 36% (35 of 97), with effects about half the original size.

cards.front: Why did Many Labs 2 weaken the excuse that replications fail because samples differ?
cards.back: Effects that were real appeared in nearly all of 125 samples across 36 countries; failed effects failed almost everywhere.

cards.front: Replication vs reproducibility: what is the difference?
cards.back: Reproducibility: same data, same analysis, same answer. Replicability: new data, same answer.

cards.front: What does a p-value actually measure?
cards.back: How often data this extreme would appear if there were no real effect. Not the chance the hypothesis is true.

cards.front: Who popularised the 5% significance threshold in 1925?
cards.back: Ronald Fisher, in 'Statistical Methods for Research Workers'.

cards.front: Cohen's d of 0.2, 0.5, 0.8: what labels?
cards.back: Small, medium, large.

cards.front: What did Jacob Cohen find in 1962 about typical psychology studies?
cards.back: Average power to detect a medium effect was about 0.48, a coin flip.

cards.front: How did Peirce and Jastrow randomise their 1884 weight experiment?
cards.back: By drawing from a shuffled pack of playing cards, with the judge blind to the order.

cards.front: Who founded the first psychology laboratory, in Leipzig in 1879?
cards.back: Wilhelm Wundt.

cards.front: What happened when Ebbinghaus's forgetting curve was replicated in 2015?
cards.back: It came back closely matching the 1880s original, from one subject relearning nonsense syllables for about 70 hours.

cards.front: What was this horse actually responding to?
cards.back: Clever Hans read tiny unconscious cues in the questioner's head and body.

cards.front: What did Levitt and List find when they reanalysed the original Hawthorne lighting data?
cards.back: The famous effect was much weaker than the legend.

cards.front: What experiment is diagrammed here?
cards.back: Milgram's obedience experiment: experimenter, teacher, learner.

cards.front: How did Milgram's archives change the 65% obedience figure?
cards.back: It was one version of more than 20; full obedience ranged from near zero to over 90%.

cards.front: Which 1971 study is this?
cards.back: The Stanford prison experiment.

cards.front: Why is the Stanford prison experiment no longer seen as valid evidence about human nature?
cards.back: Archives show guards were told what was expected and coached to be tough: demand characteristics.

cards.front: What did the 2018 marshmallow test replication find?
cards.back: The link to later achievement was about half as big, and near zero after accounting for family background.

cards.front: What does this card test?
cards.back: Conformity: Asch's line-judgment task.

cards.front: Ego depletion: what effect size did the 2016 23-lab replication find?
cards.back: d = 0.04, essentially zero, against 0.62 in a 2010 meta-analysis.

cards.front: What is she demonstrating?
cards.back: A power pose (Amy Cuddy, 2011).

cards.front: What did Dana Carney, first author of the power pose study, say in 2016?
cards.back: 'I do not believe that power pose effects are real.'

cards.front: Why did the 'elderly walking' priming effect appear only sometimes in 2012?
cards.back: It appeared when experimenters expected it and timed walking by hand: the experimenters, not the words.

cards.front: The tendency for the first, threshold-crossing estimate of an effect to be too large is called the ___.

cards.front: What is HARKing?
cards.back: Hypothesising After the Results are Known: presenting a post hoc idea as if predicted.

cards.front: What does a lopsided chart like this suggest?
cards.back: Publication bias: small studies with null results are missing (asymmetric funnel plot).

cards.back: About 91.5%, the highest of any field.

cards.back: A paper accepted on its question and method before results exist; published whatever the outcome.
