best_facts.fact: A 2011 experiment showed that listening to 'When I'm Sixty-Four' made people 1.5 years younger by birth date, with p = .04. It was built to show how ordinary analysis habits can prove the impossible.
best_facts.why_surprising: A correct-looking statistical result for a physically impossible claim.

best_facts.fact: When 100 psychology studies were repeated in 2015, only 36% of significant results came back significant, and average effects were about half the size.
best_facts.why_surprising: Two thirds of findings in leading journals did not repeat.

best_facts.fact: A paper by leading reformers arguing that rigorous methods produce 86% replication was itself retracted in 2024, for not following its own preregistration.
best_facts.why_surprising: The reformers were caught by their own rules.

best_facts.fact: A study on how signing an honesty pledge makes people honest turned out to rest on fabricated car-insurance data, with mileages spread as evenly as a random number generator.
best_facts.why_surprising: Fraud in a study of honesty.

best_facts.fact: Ebbinghaus tested only himself in the 1880s, yet his forgetting curve replicated closely in 2015, while many modern studies with hundreds of people did not.
best_facts.why_surprising: A sample of one beat big flashy studies.

best_facts.fact: The 'elderly priming' walking effect vanished when timed by infrared sensors, but reappeared when experimenters expected it and used stopwatches.
best_facts.why_surprising: The effect lived in the experimenters, not the participants.

best_facts.fact: 96% of subjects in top psychology journals (2003 to 2007) came from Western industrialised countries with about 12% of the world's people.
best_facts.why_surprising: 'Human nature' was largely American undergraduate nature.

best_facts.fact: A random American undergraduate was about 4,000 times more likely to be a psychology research subject than a random person outside the West.
best_facts.why_surprising: The scale of the sampling skew.

best_facts.fact: Ego depletion was supported by hundreds of studies and a 2010 meta-analysis of d = 0.62, then a 23-lab test found d = 0.04.
best_facts.why_surprising: A large literature can stand on almost nothing.

best_facts.fact: Standard psychology papers report support for their first hypothesis 96% of the time; Registered Reports, accepted before results, only 44%.
best_facts.why_surprising: Hiding nulls more than doubles the apparent success rate.

best_facts.fact: In 2020, analysis of 219 CCTV-recorded street fights in three countries found a bystander intervened in about nine of ten, contradicting the Kitty Genovese legend.
best_facts.why_surprising: Real crowds help far more than textbooks implied.

best_facts.fact: Cyril Burt's twin IQ correlation stayed at exactly 0.771 to three decimal places as his sample size changed.
best_facts.why_surprising: Real data never stay that still.

best_facts.fact: None of the 193 cancer biology experiments chosen for replication was described in enough detail to repeat without asking the original authors.
best_facts.why_surprising: Published methods were not enough to redo the work.

best_facts.fact: In rural Uttar Pradesh, low-caste boys solved mazes as well as high-caste boys until their caste was read aloud, when a gap of about 25% opened.
Prediction markets where psychologists bet on replications called the outcome correctly about 71% of the time.
best_facts.why_surprising: Experts could sense which findings were weak before anyone checked.

best_facts.fact: In 2025 nine of the ten institutions with the highest research-integrity risk scores worldwide were Indian universities.
best_facts.why_surprising: India's research boom has a hidden quality problem.

best_facts.fact: Psychology's first randomised, blinded experiment, in 1884, used a shuffled pack of playing cards to set the order of weights.
best_facts.why_surprising: Randomisation came to psychology decades before it reached medicine.

best_facts.fact: Brian Wansink's downfall began with his own 2016 blog post praising a student for squeezing results out of a 'failed' dataset.
best_facts.why_surprising: He described p-hacking as good practice, in public.

side_dish.title: The verb that changed what witnesses saw
side_dish.body_md:
In 1974 the psychologists **Elizabeth Loftus** and John Palmer showed students film clips of car crashes, then asked how fast the cars were going when they 'hit' each other. For some students the verb was 'smashed', for others 'collided', 'bumped' or 'contacted'. One word changed the answers. 'Smashed' produced an average estimate of about 41 miles per hour; 'contacted' about 32. A week later, students asked the 'smashed' question were more than twice as likely to remember seeing broken glass. There was none.

This is one of psychology's sturdiest findings, replicated in many forms for 50 years: memory is rebuilt each time it is recalled, and questions can quietly rewrite it. Loftus went on to show in 1995 that about a quarter of adults could be led to 'remember' being lost in a shopping mall as a child, an event that never happened.

The courtroom consequences are large. In the United States, the Innocence Project reports that eyewitness misidentification played a role in roughly 69% of the more than 375 wrongful convictions later overturned by DNA evidence. Police forces now use reforms drawn straight from experimental psychology: blind line-ups, where the officer does not know who the suspect is (the Clever Hans fix), recording a witness's confidence at the first identification, and neutral instructions.

The connection to today: a robust, replicated finding, built on random assignment and careful wording, changed how justice works.

offline_task.title: Replicate the Stroop effect at your table
offline_task.body_md:
You will run one of psychology's most replicated experiments, with a stopwatch and two sheets of paper.

1. On sheet A, write 20 colour words (RED, GREEN, BLUE, YELLOW) with markers whose ink **matches** the word. On sheet B, write the same 20 words, each in a **mismatched** ink: RED in green, BLUE in yellow, and so on.
2. Recruit at least five people. **Randomise** who does A first and who does B first by tossing a coin, so practice does not favour one sheet.
3. Ask each person to name the **ink colours**, not the words, as fast as possible. Time each sheet. Count errors.
4. Before you start, write down your prediction and how you will compare the sheets: average time for A against average time for B. That is your **preregistration**.
5. Compare. Stroop's 1935 subjects took about 74% longer on conflicting colours.

Then ask: did everyone show the effect? How big was it? Would five people have been enough to detect a subtle effect? Note your answers in a line or two.
